problem: Prior spoken human-robot dialogue systems (e.g. ScoutBot) handle only a single robot, and mostly rely on wizards or predefined grammars, so they cannot study dialogue with multiple heterogeneous robots (ground and aerial).
motivation: In time-critical settings such as search and rescue, natural language is a hands-free single interface to a multi-robot team, but research needs a flexible platform and data-collection tooling. The paper builds on ScoutBot and earlier Wizard-of-Oz experiments to extend to multiple robots.
key_idea: A modular, wizard-swappable platform (MultiBot) that pairs off-the-shelf ASR and NPCEditor dialogue management with a Tactical Behavior Specification (TBS) message layer that maps verbal instructions to robot-specific ROS behavior trees for a simulated ground and aerial robot.
insight: Routing instructions through an intermediate representation (TBS) decouples language understanding from robot-specific behaviors, so robots with different capabilities can share one language interface. Preliminary ongoing work reports that implicit addressee (task-to-robot binding learned from synthetic training data via NPCEditor) can disambiguate which robot acts without naming it, but no quantitative ablation is given.
method: Speech I/O: Google ASR for input; Festival with MBROLA voices for robot and system speech, with a chat-window fallback for noisy or stealth conditions.

NLU/DM: NPCEditor statistical retrieval dialogue manager with five instruction categories (wake, waypoint navigation, follow-behind, inspection, patrol), generating clarifications to the user and instructions to the robots.
Tactical Behavior Specification (TBS): common structured message format carrying a high-level action plus location and object info, mapped to robot-specific behaviors.
Robot behaviors: Smach finite-state-machine/behavior trees in ROS (go-to, follow, scout, search, takeoff/land), where composed instructions serve as building blocks for others.
Perception: onboard camera with a YOLO object classifier to detect objects of interest such as injured persons; the aerial robot chooses 'perch and stare' or hover.
Simulation: software-in-the-loop (SITL) simulation of a Clearpath Husky ground robot and a Snapdragon Flight quadrotor in an outdoor environment with roads and buildings.
Wizard-swappable components: human wizards can stand in for dialogue or behavior modules to collect training data.

setting.backbone: Google ASR + NPCEditor statistical dialogue retrieval + Smach behavior trees + YOLO detector
setting.training_data: Dialogue retrieval trained on Wizard-of-Oz data from prior experiments and a synthetic instruction dataset; no large-scale training reported
setting.observation: Simulated onboard camera for object detection; user speech; 2D map given to the user
setting.action_space: High-level TBS commands (go-to, follow, scout, search, takeoff/land) executed as ROS behaviors
setting.simulator: ROS software-in-the-loop simulation (outdoor environment with roads and buildings)

numbers_note: Demo paper with no quantitative evaluation or benchmark results.
results: The paper demonstrates a working end-to-end spoken dialogue system controlling two simulated robots (ground and aerial) in a search-and-rescue scenario, with a video demo. No quantitative results are reported.
limitations: No quantitative evaluation of dialogue accuracy or navigation performance; only a demonstration.
Simulation only; the explicit-addressee scheme requires naming a robot, and implicit addressing relies on synthetic training data.
